passages.title: Analgesia within 30 minutes of presentation
passages.body: Give the first dose of analgesia within 30 minutes of the person arriving at hospital. Treat an acute painful episode as a medical emergency from the moment of presentation, not from the moment a doctor first sees the patient.

passages.title: One hour standard in the ASH guideline
passages.body: The ASH 2020 pain guideline recommends rapid assessment and administration of analgesia within one hour of arrival at the emergency department, followed by frequent reassessment. Where a national target is stricter, as the 30 minute NICE target is in England, the stricter target governs local practice.

passages.title: Individualised care plans come first
passages.body: When a patient has an individualised pain plan, use the agent, route and dose written in that signed plan rather than a generic protocol. Plans are written by the specialist team who know the patient's previous responses, and following them shortens the time to effective relief.

passages.title: Ask what has already been taken
passages.body: Ask what analgesia the person has already taken for this episode, including when and how much, before choosing the first dose. Most people try their own analgesia at home before coming to hospital.

passages.title: Believe and assess the pain
passages.body: Assess pain with a validated score and accept the person's own report of how severe it is. The parliamentary inquiry found that patients were often disbelieved, labelled as drug seeking and left waiting, and that these attitudes contributed to avoidable harm.

passages.title: Strong opioid for severe pain
passages.body: Offer a bolus of a strong opioid, such as morphine or diamorphine, to people with severe pain and to those with moderate pain who have not had relief from weaker analgesia. The exact dose and route come from the individual plan or the prescriber, not from this system.

passages.title: Never use pethidine
passages.body: Do not use pethidine to treat an acute painful sickle cell episode. Its metabolite accumulates and can cause seizures, and safer strong opioids are available.

passages.title: Paracetamol as an adjunct
passages.body: Offer regular paracetamol alongside opioid analgesia unless it is contraindicated. Adjuncts reduce the total opioid needed.

passages.title: NSAIDs as an adjunct unless contraindicated
passages.body: Offer a non steroidal anti inflammatory drug as an adjunct unless it is contraindicated, for example by renal impairment. Check the individual plan, which records kidney problems and other cautions.

passages.title: Reassess pain every 30 minutes until relief
passages.body: Reassess pain every 30 minutes until satisfactory relief is reached, and then at least every four hours. Each reassessment records the pain score, sedation level and vital signs.

passages.title: Monitoring after opioids
passages.body: After giving opioids, monitor pain, sedation, vital signs, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation every 30 minutes until pain is controlled and the patient is stable, then at least every four hours. Escalate if sedation deepens or the respiratory rate falls.

passages.title: Opioid related respiratory depression
passages.body: A low respiratory rate or increasing sedation after opioids suggests opioid toxicity and needs immediate review, including whether to hold further doses and whether naloxone is needed under the local opioid safety policy. The national enquiry found inadequate monitoring of patients receiving opioids.

passages.title: Second dose and escalation
passages.body: If pain is not controlled after the first dose, give further doses in line with the individual plan and involve the haematology team early. Do not wait for the next routine review when a patient remains in severe pain.

passages.title: Ketamine as a specialist adjunct
passages.body: For pain that remains refractory to opioids, the ASH guideline suggests a low dose ketamine infusion as an adjunct, used only with specialist input and in a setting able to monitor it.

passages.title: Inform haematology on admission
passages.body: Tell the specialist haematology team when a person with sickle cell disease is admitted. Specialist review within the first day improves the management of pain and complications.

passages.title: Hydration
passages.body: Encourage oral fluids and give intravenous fluids only if the patient cannot drink enough, watching for fluid overload, which can worsen breathing problems.

passages.title: Do not transfuse uncomplicated pain
passages.body: Blood transfusion is not indicated for an uncomplicated painful episode. Consider transfusion only for specific complications, such as acute chest syndrome, stroke or severe acute anaemia, after discussion with haematology.

passages.title: Incentive spirometry while awake
passages.body: Encourage incentive spirometry while awake for patients admitted with a painful episode, particularly with chest or back pain. Regular deep breathing reduces the risk of developing acute chest syndrome.

passages.title: Acute chest syndrome definition
passages.body: Acute chest syndrome is an acute illness with fever or respiratory symptoms together with a new pulmonary infiltrate on a chest X ray. It often develops during an admission for pain rather than at presentation.

passages.title: Acute chest syndrome often develops after admission
passages.body: Many episodes of acute chest syndrome start one to three days after admission for a painful episode. Keep watching for new chest pain, cough, fever, a rising respiratory rate or falling oxygen saturation throughout the stay.

passages.title: Falling oxygen saturation
passages.body: A fall in oxygen saturation from the patient's usual level is an early warning of acute chest syndrome. Review the patient promptly, examine the chest and consider a chest X ray and blood gases.

passages.title: Chest symptoms at presentation
passages.body: Patients presenting with chest pain, breathlessness or cough need a chest X ray and oxygen saturation assessment early, and the haematology team should be told, because acute chest syndrome may already be present.

passages.title: Treating acute chest syndrome
passages.body: Treat acute chest syndrome with antibiotics that cover common and atypical organisms, such as an intravenous cephalosporin with a macrolide, supplemental oxygen to the target set by the treating team, careful analgesia and incentive spirometry.

passages.title: Transfusion in acute chest syndrome
passages.body: Transfusion is an important treatment for acute chest syndrome. Simple transfusion is used for moderate illness and exchange transfusion for severe or worsening illness, decided with the haematology team.

passages.title: Escalation to critical care
passages.body: Involve critical care early when acute chest syndrome is progressing, oxygen needs are rising or the patient is tiring. Early escalation is safer than rescue after respiratory failure.

passages.title: Opioids and acute chest syndrome
passages.body: Adequate analgesia helps breathing by reducing splinting, but excessive opioid sedation causes hypoventilation, which can contribute to acute chest syndrome. Balance pain relief against sedation and keep monitoring the respiratory rate.

passages.title: Fever is an emergency
passages.body: People with sickle cell disease and a temperature of 38.5 degrees or above need urgent evaluation, including a full blood count, reticulocyte count and blood cultures, and prompt parenteral antibiotics, because reduced splenic function raises the risk of serious infection.

passages.title: Local fever flag
passages.body: This service flags a temperature of 38.0 degrees or above for a sepsis screen, which is lower than the 38.5 degree threshold in the NHLBI report. The local threshold is a configuration setting and can be changed in the protocol file.

passages.title: Sepsis recognition
passages.body: Use structured sepsis risk assessment for anyone with suspected infection, and give antibiotics within the time set by the risk level. People with sickle cell disease have functional hyposplenism and are at higher risk.

passages.title: Neurological symptoms
passages.body: New weakness, speech disturbance, severe headache, seizure or reduced consciousness may be a stroke and need emergency assessment, urgent brain imaging and immediate haematology involvement.

passages.title: Exchange transfusion for acute stroke
passages.body: For acute stroke in sickle cell disease, urgent exchange transfusion is the standard treatment, arranged with haematology alongside the usual stroke pathway.

passages.title: Priapism
passages.body: Priapism lasting four hours or more needs urgent urology review for aspiration and irrigation, with analgesia and haematology involvement. Ask about the duration at triage because delay increases the risk of lasting damage.

passages.title: Acute anaemia
passages.body: A haemoglobin well below the patient's steady state needs explanation. Check the reticulocyte count: a low count suggests a transient red cell aplasia, and a high count with an enlarging spleen suggests splenic sequestration.

passages.title: Local haemoglobin flag
passages.body: This service flags a haemoglobin 2 g/dL or more below the recorded steady state. The value is a configuration setting, chosen to match common UK hospital protocols.

passages.title: Splenic sequestration
passages.body: Acute splenic sequestration presents with a rapidly enlarging spleen and a sharp fall in haemoglobin and can cause shock. It is more common in children and in people with HbSC or HbS beta thalassaemia, and needs urgent haematology input.

passages.title: Abdominal pain
passages.body: Abdominal pain may be a painful episode but can also be gallstones, sequestration, infection or a surgical emergency. Examine carefully and seek a surgical opinion when the picture does not fit an ordinary crisis.

passages.title: Haematology review within one day
passages.body: Every adult admitted with sickle cell disease should be reviewed by a specialist haematology team, ideally within the first day, and the team should be able to see the individual care plan.

passages.title: Plans must be accessible
passages.body: Individual care plans only help if emergency staff can see them. The national standards and the parliamentary inquiry both call for plans that are available in the emergency department record at the time of arrival.

passages.title: Review plans regularly
passages.body: Individual plans should be reviewed regularly, at least yearly, so that the recorded agent, route and cautions reflect the patient's current needs. An out of date plan should still be read but checked with haematology.

passages.title: Local plan review flag
passages.body: This service marks a plan as due for review when it was last reviewed more than 12 months ago. The plan is still shown first; the flag prompts a check with haematology.

passages.title: Delays and stigma
passages.body: The parliamentary inquiry reported long waits for pain relief and repeated assumptions that patients were drug seeking, particularly for people who attend often. Frequent attendance reflects disease severity and should never lower the priority of pain relief.

passages.title: National enquiry findings
passages.body: The national enquiry into deaths of people with sickle cell disease found delays in analgesia, inadequate monitoring after opioids and failures to recognise deterioration, and recommended better observation and earlier specialist involvement.

passages.title: Communication and partnership
passages.body: People with sickle cell disease often know their condition well. Involve them in decisions about their analgesia and listen to what has worked before.

passages.title: Observations four hourly when stable
passages.body: Once pain is controlled and the patient is stable, continue observations at least every four hours, including oxygen saturation and respiratory rate, for the rest of the admission.

passages.title: Early warning scores
passages.body: Use the hospital's early warning score with every set of observations and follow the escalation policy, while remembering that the patient's own baseline oxygen saturation may be lower than the general population.

passages.title: Baseline oxygen saturation
passages.body: Some people with sickle cell disease have a lower steady state oxygen saturation. Compare readings with the patient's own baseline as well as with fixed thresholds.

passages.title: Chest X ray when chest signs appear
passages.body: When new chest signs, cough or falling saturation appear during an admission, arrange a chest X ray promptly. Clinical signs can lag behind the radiological changes.

passages.title: Blood tests at presentation
passages.body: At presentation take a full blood count and reticulocyte count and compare them with the patient's steady state values. Do not delay analgesia while waiting for results.

passages.title: Do not delay analgesia for tests
passages.body: Do not delay the first dose of analgesia while waiting for investigations, a doctor's review or a bed. Analgesia can be started from a patient group direction or nurse led protocol where available.

passages.title: Nurse initiated analgesia
passages.body: Nurse initiated analgesia under an agreed protocol shortens the time to the first dose, especially when the department is crowded.

passages.title: Crowding and delays
passages.body: Department crowding is a major cause of delayed pain relief. A painful sickle cell episode should be prioritised at triage regardless of how busy the department is.

passages.title: Discharge planning
passages.body: Before discharge, make sure pain is controlled on oral analgesia, the patient has a supply and clear advice on when to return, and that the specialist team is informed for follow up.

passages.title: Hydroxyurea review
passages.body: People with frequent painful episodes or previous acute chest syndrome should be offered review for hydroxyurea by the specialist team, as it reduces crises and chest syndrome.

passages.title: Learning from each admission
passages.body: After each admission, update the individual plan with what worked and what did not, so the next attendance starts from better information.

passages.title: Pain that does not fit
passages.body: If the pain is different from the patient's usual crises, or does not respond as expected, look for another cause, including acute chest syndrome, infection, avascular necrosis, sequestration or a surgical problem.

passages.title: Avascular necrosis
passages.body: Persistent hip or shoulder pain may be avascular necrosis rather than a typical crisis and needs imaging and specialist review when it does not settle.

passages.title: Pain relief and breathing
passages.body: Good analgesia for chest wall and back pain helps prevent splinting and shallow breathing, which lower the risk of acute chest syndrome.

passages.title: Hypoxia and oxygen
passages.body: Give supplemental oxygen when saturation is below the target set for the patient, and investigate why. Do not use oxygen to mask a deterioration without finding its cause.

passages.title: Children are different
passages.body: This service is designed for adult emergency departments. Children with sickle cell disease follow paediatric pathways with different thresholds for fever, sequestration and stroke.

passages.title: Pregnancy
passages.body: Pregnant women with sickle cell disease presenting in pain need joint obstetric and haematology care. The general pathway in this service does not replace that.

passages.title: Deterioration model alerts
passages.body: The Crescent Vigil deterioration model estimates the chance that acute chest syndrome will be diagnosed in the next 24 hours. An alert prompts a bedside review and a check of the chest, oxygen saturation and respiratory rate; it never replaces clinical judgement.

passages.title: What the system will not do
passages.body: This system does not calculate or suggest drug doses, does not prescribe and does not replace the clinician. Doses always come from the signed individual plan or the responsible prescriber.

passages.title: Safeguarding and mental health
passages.body: If a patient expresses thoughts of self harm or appears in crisis, follow the hospital's mental health and safeguarding pathway and involve the liaison psychiatry team, while continuing to treat pain.

passages.title: Respecting refusal and preferences
passages.body: Respect the patient's stated preferences about route, for example subcutaneous rather than intravenous when venous access is difficult, which is often recorded in the plan.
